panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: CT image showing classic early ischemic signs of stroke: loss of insular ribbon and hypodensity. B: CT Perfusion maps (CBF/Tmax) indicating a mismatch pattern consistent with an acute ischemic stroke. C: CTA showing the vessel occlusion responsible for the acute stroke. D: CBF multithreshold analysis showing a defined core of dense ischemia. E: Tmax multithreshold analysis highlighting severe delayed perfusion in the surrounding tissue, indicating high risk of expansion.
panels.attribution_text: Buoso et al. RAPID perfusion CT in acute ischemic stroke: an educational pictorial review of common patterns, pearls, and pitfalls. Insights into imaging 2026. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 6.
panels.figure_caption: The “Warning Zone”—integrating technical alerts with clinical reality. Representative example of an intermediate perfusion pattern, highlighting the need for integrated interpretation of perfusion parameters, vascular findings, collateral status, and clinical presentation, in an 85-year-old female who presented with a sudden onset of motor deficit involving the left hand, which rapidly progressed to a complete left-sided motor hemisyndrome. A Axial NCCT at the level of the sylvian fissure shows early ischemic signs, including subtle loss of the insular ribbon and cortical swelling (red arrow). A hyperdense MCA sign is present (blue arrow). B CBF (CBF < 30%) and Tmax maps indicate a mismatch profile with a 21 mL core (CBF < 30%) and 82 mL of hypoperfused tissue (Tmax > 6 s). Notably, the software generates a yellow warning regarding source data quality and bolus timing. This alert necessitates a meticulous review of the concentration-time curves to exclude truncation or suboptimal contrast arrival that could skew volumetric results. C CTA MIP confirms the right M2 occlusion, with the red overlay delineating the threatened vascular territory. D Multithreshold CBF analysis shows a core volume that remains relatively stable between the < 20% (8 mL) and < 30% (21 mL) thresholds, suggesting a clearly defined area of dense ischemia. E Multithreshold Tmax analysis reveals a high Hypoperfusion Index (Tmax > 10 s/Tmax > 6 s) of 0.6. More than half of the penumbra is already critically delayed (Tmax > 10 s = 49 mL, red), signaling poor collateral recruitment and a high risk of rapid infarct expansion despite the seemingly “favorable” mismatch ratio of 3.9. This case highlights how the Hypoperfusion Index can provide a more accurate physiological snapshot than summary volumes alone

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Panel A is a DWI sequence showing restricted diffusion in the fornix, corpus callosum, and caudate nucleus of a patient with acute ischemic stroke, matching the caption description. B: Panel B is a FLAIR sequence at 1 month showing gliotic lesions evolution following an acute ischemic stroke, consistent with long-term sequelae of the target disease. C: Panel C is a DWI sequence showing acute ischemic stroke limited to the fornixal columns in the second patient. D: Panel D is a FLAIR sequence showing acute ischemic stroke restricted to the fornixal columns of the second patient.

panels.figure_caption: MRI findings of two patients with acute ischemic stroke of the fornix. In the first patient DWI sequence revealed restricted diffusion involving the columns of the fornix, the corpus callosum and the right caudate nucleus (A); these structures are included in the vascular territory of the ScA (fornix, corpus callosum) and the right RAH (caudate head). FLAIR sequence obtained at 1-month shows gliotic lesions evolution (B). In the second patient, MRI acquired at symptom onset reveals acute ischemic stroke involving only forniceal columns both in DWI (C) and FLAIR (D) sequences. Forniceal columns appear swollen as well. DWI, diffusion weighted imaging; ScA, subcallosal artery; RAH, recurrent artery of Heubner; FLAIR, fluid attenuated inversion recovery.
in_text_mentions: MRI data were available in all patients and revealed an isolated fornix involvement in 22 (52%) cases, 90% of which were bilateral. The most frequently associated involved structure was the corpus callosum (18, 45%), as expected by the vascular territory of the ScA previously described. Along with ScA involvement, 4/40 (10%) of patients had a concomitant stroke in the territory of recurrent artery of Heuber (RAH). Examples of MRI findings in two cases of acute ischemic stroke of the fornix are reported in Figure 4.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: Panel A is an axial NCCT demonstrating a hyperdense MCA sign and established ischemic changes in the left MCA territory of a 61-year-old female, consistent with acute ischemic stroke. B: Panel B displays CBF and Tmax perfusion maps from a case of acute ischemic stroke, illustrating the hypoperfused territory extent. C: Panel C is a CTA MIP showing left M1 segment occlusion, characteristic of an acute large vessel occlusion in AIS. D: Panel D is a technical visualization of multithreshold Tmax analysis applied to a patient's case, illustrating the dependency of volume estimation on threshold choice. E: Panel E displays multithreshold CBF analysis results for the patient, highlighting the discrepancy between different flow cutoffs in the acute ischemic stroke.
panels.attribution_text: Buoso et al. RAPID perfusion CT in acute ischemic stroke: an educational pictorial review of common patterns, pearls, and pitfalls. Insights into imaging 2026. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 5.
panels.figure_caption: The threshold effect—navigating Tmax and CBF Sensitivity. Representative example illustrating the influence of different Tmax thresholds on the estimation of hypoperfused tissue volume and the interpretation of penumbral extent, in a 61-year-old female presented with acute neurological deficits. A Axial NCCT at the level of the basal ganglia reveals established ischemic changes in the left MCA territory (red arrow) and a prominent hyperdense MCA sign (blue arrow), indicative of acute large vessel occlusion. B CBF (CBF < 30%) and Tmax maps using standard thresholds ($CBF$ < 30% and Tmax > 6 s). The automated summary identifies a 40 mL core and a 125 mL hypoperfused territory, yielding a mismatch ratio of 3.1. C CTA MIP demonstrates the left M1 segment occlusion, with the red overlay highlighting the downstream perfusion deficit. D Multithreshold Tmax analysis illustrates the “nested” stratification of perfusion delay. Note how the abnormal volume expands to 182 mL when using the most sensitive threshold (Tmax > 4 s, blue). The Hypoperfusion Index (Tmax > 10 s/Tmax > 6 s) of 0.4 indicates that nearly half of the penumbra is under critical hypoperfusion (Tmax >10 s = 56 mL, red), a marker of moderate collateral failure. E Multithreshold CBF analysis demonstrates that while 40 mL of tissue meets the CBF < 30% criteria, 0 mL is currently below the more severe CBF < 20% threshold. This discrepancy suggests that although an infarct core is present, the degree of flow reduction has not yet reached the most critical levels across the entire lesion, potentially defining a “gray zone” for therapeutic timing

source_variants.figure_caption: The threshold effect—navigating Tmax and CBF Sensitivity. Representative example illustrating the influence of different Tmax thresholds on the estimation of hypoperfused tissue volume and the interpretation of penumbral extent, in a 61-year-old female presented with acute neurological deficits. A Axial NCCT at the level of the basal ganglia reveals established ischemic changes in the left MCA territory (red arrow) and a prominent hyperdense MCA sign (blue arrow), indicative of acute large vessel occlusion. B CBF (CBF < 30%) and Tmax maps using standard thresholds ($CBF$ < 30% and Tmax > 6 s). The automated summary identifies a 40 mL core and a 125 mL hypoperfused territory, yielding a mismatch ratio of 3.1. C CTA MIP demonstrates the left M1 segment occlusion, with the red overlay highlighting the downstream perfusion deficit. D Multithreshold Tmax analysis illustrates the “nested” stratification of perfusion delay. Note how the abnormal volume expands to 182 mL when using the most sensitive threshold (Tmax > 4 s, blue). The Hypoperfusion Index (Tmax > 10 s/Tmax > 6 s) of 0.4 indicates that nearly half of the penumbra is under critical hypoperfusion (Tmax >10 s = 56 mL, red), a marker of moderate collateral failure. E Multithreshold CBF analysis demonstrates that while 40 mL of tissue meets the CBF < 30% criteria, 0 mL is currently below the more severe CBF < 20% threshold. This discrepancy suggests that although an infarct core is present, the degree of flow reduction has not yet reached the most critical levels across the entire lesion, potentially defining a “gray zone” for therapeutic timing

panels.figure_caption: Anatomical blind spots: the pitfall of the posterior circulation. Representative example highlighting the limited sensitivity of CT perfusion in the posterior circulation, where technical and anatomical factors may lead to false-negative RAPID results, in a 70-year-old male patient presented with acute sensory disturbances of the face and an evident deviation of the oral commissure. A Axial NCCT reveals a subtle but definitive area of low attenuation in the left cerebellar hemisphere (red arrow), though visualization is often hampered by bone-induced artifacts in this region. B CBF (CBF < 30%) and Tmax maps demonstrate a complete diagnostic failure of the automated software. Both the infarct core (CBF < 30%) and the hypoperfusion territory (Tmax > 6.0 s) are reported as 0 mL. This “false negative” is a known limitation in the posterior circulation due to lower signal-to-noise ratios and unique hemodynamics. C Multithreshold Tmax analysis shows only a minimal, non-specific volume (27 mL) at the most permissive threshold (Tmax > 4.0 s, blue). All clinical thresholds (Tmax > 6 s, > 8 s, > 10 s) are entirely negative. D, E MRI DWI and ADC Map (infratentorial) confirm an acute infarct in the left cerebellar hemisphere with marked restricted diffusion, correlating with the NCCT findings but completely missed by CTP. F, G MRI DWI and ADC map (supratentorial) demonstrate another focus in the right temporal-parietal region. This multi-territorial infarct pattern, combined with the CTP failure, underscores that in the posterior circulation, clinical judgment and MRI must override automated “zero-volume” reports to avoid catastrophic undertreatment

The 10 MCA zones designated by the ASPECTS scoring system are C caudate, L lentiform nucleus, IC internal capsule, I insular ribbon, M1–6 cortical regions (M1–3 at the level of basal ganglia, M4–6 at the level cranial to the basal ganglia). Initial DW images and their corresponding ADC maps at the basal ganglia level (a, a') and the supraganglionic level (b, b') reveal the presence of acute infarction in I, M1, M2, and M5 regions with a resultant ASPECTS score of 6. SW images at the basal ganglia level (c) and the supraganglionic level (d) reveal the presence of APVs, in terms of either density and/or caliber and/or hypointensity, in I (blue arrow) and in M1–6 regions (red, purple, gray, green, orange, and black arrows respectively) with a resultant ASPECTS score of 3 (similar colored arrows point to the corresponding areas in the contralateral normal hemisphere for comparison). DWI/SWI mismatch score is 3. Follow up FLAIR images, obtained 10 days later, at the basal ganglia level (e) and the supraganglionic level (f) reveal in addition to the originally infarcted zones, infarction growth in L, IC, and M4, giving an overall ASPECTS score of 3 and an IGS of 3. The faint hyperintensities noted at M3 and M6 zones were considered to be ischemic foci and not newly infarcted areas as they were evident in the FLAIR images of the initial MRI with no corresponding diffusion restriction
